title: No Previous Error Code / Normal Operation
shortDescription: A single blink indicates the system has no stored fault codes and is operating normally or in standby.
fullDescription: On many Lennox furnace models, a single LED blink indicates that no diagnostic fault codes are stored. The system is either in normal standby or has recently been reset. If the furnace is not heating, the issue may be in the thermostat or wiring rather than the furnace itself.
safetyWarning: Gas furnace safety: If you smell gas, leave immediately and call your gas company. Always ensure carbon monoxide detectors are installed and functional.

causes.cause: System recently reset or power cycled
Thermostat wiring issue preventing heat call

symptoms: Single LED blink on control board
Furnace in standby mode
No active heating cycle
System appears normal but not running

fixSteps.title: Check Thermostat
fixSteps.instruction: Verify the thermostat is set to HEAT mode and the set temperature is above room temperature.

fixSteps.title: Raise Temperature Setting
fixSteps.instruction: Increase the thermostat set point 5 degrees above room temperature to trigger a heat call.

fixSteps.title: Check Thermostat Wiring
fixSteps.instruction: At the furnace, verify the thermostat wires are securely connected to the correct terminals on the control board.

fixSteps.title: Test with Jumper
fixSteps.instruction: Briefly jump R and W terminals on the control board. If the furnace starts, the thermostat or its wiring is the issue.

whenToCallPro: If the furnace does not respond to a thermostat call and jumper test fails to start the system.

faq.q: Is one blink an error on my Lennox furnace?
faq.a: No, on most Lennox models one blink means no fault codes are stored. It indicates normal standby operation.

faq.q: Why is my Lennox furnace not starting with 1 blink?
faq.a: One blink means the furnace control board is OK. Check your thermostat settings, batteries, and wiring.

faq.q: Should I call for service with 1 blink?
faq.a: Not typically. One blink is not an error. Only call if the furnace fails to start when the thermostat calls for heat.

title: System Lockout — Retries Exceeded
shortDescription: The furnace has locked out after failing to ignite within the allowed number of retries.
fullDescription: Two LED blinks on a Lennox furnace indicate the system has locked out due to failed ignition attempts. The control board attempted to ignite the burners multiple times without success. The lockout will automatically reset after approximately one hour, or can be manually reset by cycling power.
safetyWarning: Gas furnace safety: If you smell gas, leave immediately and call your gas company. Do not repeatedly attempt to reset the furnace if it continues to lock out, as this may indicate a gas or ignition system issue.

causes.cause: Dirty or failing hot surface igniter
Dirty flame sensor not detecting flame
Gas supply issue or closed gas valve

symptoms: Two LED blinks on control board
Furnace not producing heat
System attempted ignition but failed
Burners may have briefly lit then gone out
Lockout lasts about one hour before auto-reset

fixSteps.title: Reset the Furnace
fixSteps.instruction: Turn off the furnace power switch, wait 30 seconds, and turn it back on. Observe the ignition sequence.

fixSteps.title: Clean the Flame Sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Locate the flame sensor (thin metal rod in the burner area). Remove it and gently clean with fine emery cloth or steel wool. Reinstall.

fixSteps.title: Inspect the Igniter
fixSteps.instruction: Check the igniter for cracks. During the ignition cycle, it should glow bright orange/white. If it glows dimly or not at all, replacement is needed.

fixSteps.title: Verify Gas Supply
fixSteps.instruction: Confirm the manual gas shutoff valve on the supply line is fully open. Check that other gas appliances work.

whenToCallPro: If the furnace locks out repeatedly after cleaning the flame sensor and checking the igniter, or if you suspect a gas supply issue.

faq.q: How long does a Lennox lockout last?
faq.a: The auto-reset lockout typically lasts about one hour. You can manually reset sooner by cycling the furnace power off and on.

faq.q: Why does my Lennox furnace keep locking out?
faq.a: Repeated lockouts usually indicate a dirty flame sensor, failing igniter, or gas supply issue. Clean the flame sensor first as it is the most common cause.

faq.q: How do I clean a Lennox flame sensor?
faq.a: Turn off the furnace, remove the single screw holding the flame sensor, and gently clean the metal rod with fine emery cloth. Do not use sandpaper or anything abrasive.

title: Pressure Switch Error
shortDescription: The pressure switch did not close or opened unexpectedly during operation.
fullDescription: Three blinks on a Lennox furnace indicate a pressure switch fault. Either the switch failed to close after the draft inducer started, or it opened during the heating cycle. This safety device verifies proper venting before and during combustion.
safetyWarning: Gas furnace safety: Never bypass the pressure switch. It ensures combustion gases are properly vented. If you smell gas, evacuate and call your gas company.

causes.cause: Blocked exhaust or intake vent pipe
Cracked or disconnected pressure switch hose

symptoms: Three LED blinks on control board
Draft inducer runs but burners do not light
Furnace starts then shuts down mid-cycle
Clicking sound from pressure switch area

fixSteps.title: Check Vent Pipes Outside
fixSteps.instruction: Inspect the exhaust and intake PVC pipes on the exterior of your home. Remove any ice, snow, bird nests, leaves, or debris blocking the openings.

fixSteps.title: Inspect Pressure Hose
fixSteps.instruction: Check the small rubber tube connecting the pressure switch to the draft inducer housing. Ensure both ends are connected and the hose has no cracks or water inside.

fixSteps.title: Clear Condensate Drain
fixSteps.instruction: On high-efficiency Lennox furnaces, check the condensate drain trap and line for clogs. Flush with warm water.

fixSteps.title: Test Pressure Switch
fixSteps.instruction: With the inducer running, check for continuity across the pressure switch with a multimeter. It should close (show continuity) when the inducer is running.

whenToCallPro: If vent pipes are clear, hose is intact, and the pressure switch still does not close. The draft inducer motor or switch may need replacement.

faq.q: Why does this happen in cold weather?
faq.a: Freezing temperatures can cause ice to form in the exhaust vent pipe, blocking airflow and triggering the pressure switch error.

faq.q: Can I bypass the pressure switch to get heat?
faq.a: Absolutely not. The pressure switch ensures combustion gases vent outside. Bypassing it risks carbon monoxide buildup in your home.

faq.q: How much does a pressure switch cost?
faq.a: A Lennox pressure switch costs $25-$60 for the part. Professional replacement runs $150-$300 total.

title: Open High Limit or Auxiliary Limit Switch
shortDescription: A temperature limit switch has tripped due to overheating.
fullDescription: Four blinks on a Lennox furnace indicate that a high limit or auxiliary limit switch has opened due to excessive temperature. The furnace overheated and the safety switch shut down the burners to prevent damage to the heat exchanger.
safetyWarning: Gas furnace safety: Repeated overheating can crack the heat exchanger, leading to potential carbon monoxide leakage. Ensure CO detectors are working. If the limit switch trips repeatedly, stop using the furnace until the cause is found.

causes.cause: Blocked return or supply air vents
Blower motor failure or weak capacitor

symptoms: Four LED blinks on control board
Furnace runs briefly then shuts off
Very hot air from vents before shutdown
Burning smell from furnace area
Furnace short-cycles repeatedly

fixSteps.title: Replace Air Filter
fixSteps.instruction: Check and replace the furnace air filter immediately. A clogged filter is the number one cause of overheating.

fixSteps.title: Open All Vents
fixSteps.instruction: Walk through your home and ensure all supply and return vents are fully open and not blocked by furniture or curtains.

fixSteps.title: Check Blower Operation
fixSteps.instruction: Set the thermostat fan to ON (continuous). The blower should run. If it does not, the blower motor or capacitor may be faulty.

fixSteps.title: Inspect Blower Wheel
fixSteps.instruction: Turn off power and inspect the blower wheel for heavy dust or debris buildup. A dirty blower wheel significantly reduces airflow.

whenToCallPro: If the filter is clean, vents are open, and the furnace still overheats. The blower motor, capacitor, or heat exchanger may need inspection.

faq.q: Can I reset the limit switch?
faq.a: Some Lennox limit switches auto-reset when the furnace cools down. Others have a manual reset button. The switch resets, but the underlying cause must still be addressed.

faq.q: How often should I change the filter?
faq.a: Check monthly, replace every 1-3 months for standard filters. If you have pets or allergies, check more frequently.

faq.q: Is overheating dangerous?
faq.a: Yes, repeated overheating can crack the heat exchanger, which can leak carbon monoxide. Address the cause promptly and ensure CO detectors are working.

title: Flame Sensed When No Flame Should Be Present
shortDescription: The flame sensor detects flame when the gas valve should be closed.
fullDescription: Five blinks on a Lennox furnace indicate that the flame sensing circuit is detecting a flame signal when the gas valve has not been energized. This is a safety lockout condition that could indicate a leaking gas valve or a wiring fault in the flame sensor circuit.
safetyWarning: CRITICAL: This code may indicate a gas valve that is not fully closing. If you smell gas, evacuate immediately and call 911 or your gas company. Do not attempt DIY repair of this condition.

causes.cause: Gas valve not closing fully (internal leak)
Flame sensor wire shorted to ground
Faulty control board flame sensing circuit

symptoms: Five LED blinks on control board
Furnace locked out and will not start
Possible gas odor (evacuate if detected)
Error occurs before ignition sequence begins

fixSteps.title: Check for Gas Odor
fixSteps.instruction: Carefully check for any gas smell near the furnace. If detected, leave immediately and call emergency services.

fixSteps.title: Power Cycle
fixSteps.instruction: Turn off furnace power and gas valve. Wait 5 minutes. Restore gas, then power. If the code returns immediately, do not attempt further troubleshooting.

fixSteps.title: Check Flame Sensor Wiring
fixSteps.instruction: With power off, inspect the flame sensor wire for damage or places where it may be touching the furnace chassis (grounding out).

fixSteps.title: Call for Professional Service
fixSteps.instruction: This code requires professional diagnosis. A technician will test the gas valve, flame sensing circuit, and control board.

whenToCallPro: Immediately. This is a safety-critical code that requires professional diagnosis and repair.

faq.q: Is this code dangerous?
faq.a: Potentially yes. It may indicate a gas valve that is not fully closing. Have it inspected by a professional promptly.

faq.q: Can I fix this myself?
faq.a: No. Gas valve and flame sensing circuit issues require professional repair for safety.

faq.q: How much will repair cost?
faq.a: If a gas valve replacement is needed, expect $200-$800 depending on the model and labor costs in your area.

title: Line Voltage Polarity or Ground Fault
shortDescription: Incorrect wiring polarity or missing ground detected.
fullDescription: Six blinks on a Lennox furnace indicate the control board has detected reversed line voltage polarity or a grounding issue. Correct polarity is essential for the flame sensing circuit to work properly.
safetyWarning: Gas furnace safety: Turn off power at the breaker before inspecting electrical connections. Incorrect wiring can be a shock hazard.

causes.cause: Hot and neutral wires reversed at furnace
Polarity reversed at the breaker panel or outlet
Control board polarity detection circuit fault

symptoms: Six LED blinks on control board
Furnace will not operate
May occur after recent electrical work
Flame sensor fails to detect flame if polarity incorrect

fixSteps.title: Turn Off Power
fixSteps.instruction: Switch off the furnace breaker before inspecting any wiring.

fixSteps.title: Check Polarity at Furnace
fixSteps.instruction: Verify the hot (black) and neutral (white) wires are connected correctly at the furnace power junction. Use a voltage tester.

fixSteps.title: Verify Ground
fixSteps.instruction: Ensure the ground wire is securely connected to the furnace chassis and runs back to the panel ground bus.

fixSteps.title: Test Outlet Polarity
fixSteps.instruction: If the furnace plugs into an outlet, use an outlet tester to verify correct polarity and grounding.

whenToCallPro: If you are not comfortable working with electrical wiring or if correcting polarity does not resolve the error.

faq.q: Why does my furnace need correct polarity?
faq.a: The flame sensing circuit requires proper polarity to detect the flame. With reversed polarity, the sensor cannot sense the flame, causing ignition failures.

faq.q: Did my electrician wire it wrong?
faq.a: It is possible. If this code appeared after recent electrical work, have the wiring checked.

faq.q: What tool do I need to check polarity?
faq.a: An outlet tester ($10-15) or a multimeter can verify polarity. Both are available at hardware stores.

title: Gas Valve or Igniter Circuit Fault
shortDescription: The control board detected an issue with the gas valve or igniter electrical circuit.
fullDescription: Seven blinks on a Lennox furnace indicate an electrical fault in the gas valve or igniter circuit. The control board cannot properly energize these components for safe ignition.
safetyWarning: Gas furnace safety: Do not attempt to manually open or adjust the gas valve. If you smell gas, leave immediately and call your gas company.

causes.cause: Loose wiring at gas valve or igniter

symptoms: Seven LED blinks on control board
No ignition attempt
Draft inducer may run but igniter does not glow
Furnace locked out

fixSteps.title: Check Igniter
fixSteps.instruction: Inspect the hot surface igniter for visible cracks. Test resistance with a multimeter (should read 10-200 ohms).

fixSteps.title: Check Wiring Connections
fixSteps.instruction: Ensure all wire connectors at the igniter and gas valve are firmly seated with no corrosion.

fixSteps.title: Test Gas Valve Coil
fixSteps.instruction: Measure resistance across the gas valve coil terminals. Compare to spec (typically 10-60 ohms). An open reading indicates a failed coil.

fixSteps.title: Replace Failed Component
fixSteps.instruction: Replace the igniter or gas valve as indicated by testing. Gas valve replacement should be done by a licensed technician.

whenToCallPro: For gas valve replacement or if testing indicates a control board fault.

faq.q: Can I replace the igniter myself?
faq.a: Yes, the igniter is a common DIY repair. Use the exact OEM part number for your Lennox model. Do not touch the element with bare hands.

faq.q: Is this the same as a lockout?
faq.a: It is different from a lockout. This indicates a circuit fault rather than failed ignition attempts. The system detects the fault before attempting ignition.

faq.q: How much does a Lennox igniter cost?
faq.a: OEM Lennox igniters typically cost $30-$80. Universal replacements are less expensive but may not fit perfectly.

title: Igniter Circuit Open
shortDescription: The hot surface igniter circuit is open, indicating a broken igniter element.
fullDescription: Eight blinks on a Lennox furnace specifically indicate that the hot surface igniter has an open circuit — the heating element is broken or has a fracture that prevents current flow. The igniter cannot heat up to ignite the gas.
safetyWarning: Gas furnace safety: Turn off the furnace before handling the igniter. The igniter is fragile and reaches extremely high temperatures during operation.

causes.cause: Igniter damaged during filter change or maintenance

symptoms: Eight LED blinks on control board
Igniter does not glow at all
Draft inducer runs but no ignition occurs
Furnace shuts down after inducer pre-purge

fixSteps.title: Visual Inspection
fixSteps.instruction: Turn off the furnace and visually inspect the igniter for cracks. Even hairline cracks can cause an open circuit.

fixSteps.title: Check Connections
fixSteps.instruction: Ensure the igniter wire connector is firmly seated. Wiggle the connection to check for intermittent contact.

fixSteps.title: Test Resistance
fixSteps.instruction: Disconnect the igniter and measure resistance. A good igniter reads 10-200 ohms. OL (open line) confirms it is broken.

fixSteps.title: Replace Igniter
fixSteps.instruction: Remove the mounting screw, disconnect the old igniter, install the new one. Handle only by the ceramic base — never touch the element.

whenToCallPro: If you are not comfortable accessing the burner compartment or if a new igniter does not resolve the issue.

faq.q: How do I know which igniter to buy?
faq.a: Use your Lennox model number (found on the data plate inside the furnace) to order the exact OEM igniter. Cross-reference part numbers online.

faq.q: Can I use a universal igniter?
faq.a: Universal igniters may work but the mounting bracket and connector may not match perfectly. OEM parts are recommended.

faq.q: How long does an igniter last?
faq.a: Typically 3-7 years. Silicon nitride igniters last longer than older silicon carbide types.

title: Low Flame Signal / Weak Flame
shortDescription: The flame sensor is detecting a weak or marginal flame signal.
fullDescription: Nine blinks on a Lennox furnace indicate that the flame sensor is reading a low microamp signal, meaning the flame is weak or the sensor is not detecting the flame properly. The furnace may operate intermittently or shut down during a heating cycle.
safetyWarning: Gas furnace safety: A weak flame can indicate incomplete combustion which produces carbon monoxide. Ensure CO detectors are working and call a professional if the problem persists.

causes.cause: Cracked or deteriorated flame sensor insulator

symptoms: Nine LED blinks on control board
Furnace starts but shuts off after a few seconds
Intermittent heating — sometimes works, sometimes does not
Flame appears weak, yellow, or flickering

fixSteps.title: Clean the Flame Sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Remove the flame sensor and clean the metal rod with fine emery cloth until shiny. This is the most common fix for low flame signal.

fixSteps.title: Inspect Sensor Insulator
fixSteps.instruction: Check the ceramic insulator around the flame sensor for cracks that could allow the signal to ground out.

fixSteps.title: Observe Flame Color
fixSteps.instruction: Watch the burner flames during operation. They should be mostly blue with small yellow tips. All-yellow or wavering flames indicate a combustion issue.

fixSteps.title: Have Gas Pressure Checked
fixSteps.instruction: A technician can measure the manifold gas pressure to ensure it is within the manufacturer's specification for your furnace.

whenToCallPro: If cleaning the flame sensor does not resolve the issue, or if the flame appears yellow or abnormal.

faq.q: What is a normal flame sensor reading?
faq.a: A healthy flame sensor typically reads 1.5-6 microamps. Below 1 microamp is considered weak and will cause intermittent shutdowns.

faq.q: How often should I clean the flame sensor?
faq.a: Clean it annually as part of routine furnace maintenance. If your furnace frequently shuts down, clean it as needed.

faq.q: Can a dirty flame sensor cause high gas bills?
faq.a: Indirectly, yes. If the furnace frequently shuts down and restarts, it runs inefficiently and uses more gas.

title: Rollout Switch Open
shortDescription: The flame rollout safety switch has tripped, indicating flames are escaping the combustion chamber.
fullDescription: Ten blinks on a Lennox furnace indicate the rollout limit switch has opened. This switch is located near the burners and detects if flames are rolling out of the combustion chamber, which is extremely dangerous. This typically indicates a blocked heat exchanger or cracked heat exchanger.
safetyWarning: CRITICAL SAFETY WARNING: Flame rollout is a serious condition. It can indicate a cracked or blocked heat exchanger, which risks carbon monoxide exposure and fire. Do not attempt to reset the rollout switch and continue operating the furnace. Call a professional immediately.
symptoms: Ten LED blinks on control board
Visible flame outside burner compartment
Scorch marks on furnace cabinet near burners
Strong burning smell
CO detectors may alarm

fixSteps.title: Turn Off the Furnace
fixSteps.instruction: Immediately turn off the furnace at both the power switch and gas supply valve. Do not attempt to reset the rollout switch.

fixSteps.title: Check for CO
fixSteps.instruction: If your carbon monoxide detectors are alarming, evacuate the home immediately and call 911.

fixSteps.title: Check Exhaust Vent
fixSteps.instruction: Visually inspect the exhaust vent pipe for obvious blockages. Do not restart the furnace even if you find and clear a blockage.

fixSteps.title: Call for Professional Inspection
fixSteps.instruction: A licensed HVAC technician must inspect the heat exchanger and determine the cause of flame rollout before the furnace can be safely operated.

whenToCallPro: Immediately. Do not operate the furnace until a professional has inspected and cleared it.

faq.q: What is flame rollout?
faq.a: Flame rollout occurs when flames escape the combustion chamber, often due to a blockage in the heat exchanger or exhaust system. It is a serious fire and CO hazard.

faq.q: Can I just reset the rollout switch?
faq.a: While some rollout switches have a manual reset button, you should never reset it without first having a professional determine and fix the cause. Operating the furnace with an unresolved rollout condition is extremely dangerous.

faq.q: How much does heat exchanger replacement cost?
faq.a: Heat exchanger replacement costs $1,000-$3,000+. If the furnace is old, replacement of the entire furnace may be more cost-effective.

title: Normal Standby / Waiting for Heat Call
shortDescription: The amber LED blinking slowly indicates normal standby operation.
fullDescription: On Lennox furnaces with a multi-color LED, a slow amber blink typically indicates normal standby — the system is powered, all safety checks are passed, and it is waiting for the thermostat to call for heat.
safetyWarning: Gas furnace safety: Even in standby, ensure the furnace area is clear of stored items and flammable materials.

causes.cause: Room temperature at or above thermostat setting
Thermostat in off or cool mode

symptoms: Slow amber LED blink
Furnace idle
System responsive to thermostat changes
No error present

fixSteps.title: Verify Thermostat
fixSteps.instruction: Check that the thermostat is set to HEAT and the set temperature is above the current room temperature.

fixSteps.title: Raise Set Point
fixSteps.instruction: Increase the set point 5 degrees above room temp. The furnace should start within 1-2 minutes.

fixSteps.title: Check Thermostat Mode
fixSteps.instruction: Ensure the thermostat is not in OFF, COOL, or AUTO mode (if cooling is not needed).

fixSteps.title: Check Programming
fixSteps.instruction: Review thermostat programming and schedules to ensure they match your heating needs.

whenToCallPro: Only if the furnace does not start when the thermostat calls for heat.

faq.q: Is slow amber blinking normal?
faq.a: Yes, it means the system is in normal standby, powered on and ready to heat when called.

faq.q: Why does my Lennox have an amber LED?
faq.a: Many Lennox models use multi-color LEDs — amber for standby, green for normal operation, and red for errors. The color and pattern depend on the model.

faq.q: Should I be concerned about the slow amber blink?
faq.a: No, this is the normal standby indicator. The furnace is operating correctly.

title: Normal Heating — Flame Detected
shortDescription: A fast green blink indicates the furnace is in normal heating operation with flame successfully detected.
fullDescription: On Lennox furnaces with multi-color LEDs, a rapidly blinking green LED indicates normal heating operation. The burners are lit, flame is detected, and the system is running a normal heating cycle.
safetyWarning: Gas furnace safety: During normal operation, ensure nothing is stored on or near the furnace, and that CO detectors are installed and working.

causes.cause: Normal heating operation — not an error
If home is not warming, may have duct or airflow issue
Thermostat set point may need adjustment
Short cycling if green blink is intermittent

symptoms: Fast green LED blink on control board
Warm air from supply vents
Normal furnace operating sounds
Thermostat shows system is running

fixSteps.title: Confirm Normal Operation
fixSteps.instruction: Verify warm air is coming from supply vents throughout the home.

fixSteps.title: Check Airflow
fixSteps.instruction: If heat seems weak, check and replace the air filter. Ensure vents are open.

fixSteps.title: Monitor Cycle Length
fixSteps.instruction: A normal cycle should last 10-20 minutes. Very short or very long cycles may indicate an issue.

fixSteps.title: Check Temperature Rise
fixSteps.instruction: Measure the temperature at a supply vent and the return vent. The difference should be 40-70 degrees F for most furnaces.

whenToCallPro: If the furnace runs but the home does not warm adequately, or if you notice abnormal cycle lengths.

faq.q: Is fast green blinking an error?
faq.a: No, on Lennox furnaces with color LEDs, fast green blinking means the furnace is heating normally.

faq.q: How do I know if my furnace is heating efficiently?
faq.a: Check the temperature rise (supply minus return air temperature). It should match the range on your furnace data plate, typically 40-70 degrees F.

faq.q: Why is my house still cold if the furnace is running?
faq.a: Check for dirty filter, closed vents, duct leaks, or an undersized system. If the furnace is heating but the house is cold, the issue is likely in air distribution.

title: Control Board Failure / Hardware Fault
shortDescription: A continuous red LED indicates an internal control board failure requiring board replacement.
fullDescription: A continuous (non-blinking) red LED on a Lennox furnace indicates an internal hardware fault on the control board itself. The board has detected an irrecoverable error in its own circuitry and cannot operate the furnace.
safetyWarning: Gas furnace safety: Turn off the furnace and gas supply. A failed control board cannot manage safety circuits, so the furnace should not be operated until repaired.

causes.cause: Failed control board component (relay, capacitor, processor)
Control board overheated from nearby heat source
Moisture or corrosion damage to the board

symptoms: Continuous red LED — no blinking pattern
Furnace completely non-functional
No response to thermostat commands
May have occurred after power outage or storm

fixSteps.title: Power Cycle
fixSteps.instruction: Turn off the furnace power for 60 seconds and restore. If the continuous red LED returns, the board has failed.

fixSteps.title: Check for Visible Damage
fixSteps.instruction: Look at the control board for burn marks, bulging capacitors, or signs of moisture damage.

fixSteps.title: Check Board Fuse
fixSteps.instruction: Verify the small fuse on the control board is intact. Replace if blown, then test again.

fixSteps.title: Replace Control Board
fixSteps.instruction: Control board replacement is typically a professional repair. The board must match the furnace model exactly and may require configuration.

whenToCallPro: Call a professional for control board replacement. This is not a typical DIY repair.

faq.q: How much does a Lennox control board cost?
faq.a: Lennox control boards typically cost $150-$500 for the part, with total installed cost of $250-$800 depending on the model.

faq.q: Can a power surge damage the control board?
faq.a: Yes, power surges from lightning or utility issues can damage electronic components on the control board. Consider a whole-house surge protector.

faq.q: Is it worth replacing the control board?
faq.a: If the furnace is less than 15 years old, board replacement is usually worthwhile. For older furnaces, compare the repair cost to replacement cost.

title: No Power to Control Board
shortDescription: The diagnostic LED is completely off, indicating no power reaching the control board.
fullDescription: When no LED is visible on the Lennox furnace control board, the board is not receiving electrical power. This could be due to a tripped breaker, blown fuse, open power switch, or failed transformer.
safetyWarning: Gas furnace safety: Turn off the gas supply valve before troubleshooting electrical issues. If you smell gas at any time, leave and call your gas company.
symptoms: No LED visible on control board
Furnace completely unresponsive
Thermostat may be blank
No sounds from furnace at all

fixSteps.title: Check Breaker
fixSteps.instruction: Locate the furnace breaker in your electrical panel. Reset it if tripped.

fixSteps.title: Check Power Switch
fixSteps.instruction: Find the power switch near the furnace (looks like a light switch) and ensure it is ON.

fixSteps.title: Check Board Fuse
fixSteps.instruction: Open the furnace panel and inspect the small fuse on the control board. Replace if blown with the same amperage.

fixSteps.title: Test Transformer
fixSteps.instruction: Measure 24VAC output from the transformer secondary. If absent with 120V present on the primary, the transformer has failed.

whenToCallPro: If the breaker trips repeatedly, or if the transformer or board has failed.

faq.q: Why does the fuse keep blowing?
faq.a: A repeatedly blown board fuse usually indicates a short circuit in the thermostat wiring. Check for damaged wires or a shorted thermostat.

faq.q: Where is the furnace power switch?
faq.a: It is usually mounted on or near the furnace, often at the top of the unit. It resembles a standard light switch.

faq.q: Can a bad thermostat blow the fuse?
faq.a: Yes, a short circuit in the thermostat or its wiring can blow the low-voltage fuse on the furnace control board.

title: Rollout Switch Requires Manual Reset
shortDescription: The flame rollout switch tripped and has a manual reset button that must be pressed.
fullDescription: Eleven blinks on some Lennox models indicate the rollout switch with manual reset has tripped. This switch must be manually reset by pressing its button after the cause of rollout has been determined and fixed.
safetyWarning: Gas furnace safety: If you smell gas, leave immediately and call your gas company.
symptoms: 11-blink LED pattern
System malfunction
No heat or intermittent heat
Unusual sounds or behavior

fixSteps.title: Power Cycle
fixSteps.instruction: Turn off furnace power for 30 seconds, then restore.

fixSteps.title: Check Filter
fixSteps.instruction: Replace the air filter if dirty.

fixSteps.title: Inspect Wiring
fixSteps.instruction: Check for loose connections.

fixSteps.title: Call Professional
fixSteps.instruction: If error persists, professional diagnosis is needed.

whenToCallPro: If basic troubleshooting does not resolve the error.

faq.q: What does 11-blink mean?
faq.a: The flame rollout switch tripped and has a manual reset button that must be pressed.

faq.q: Is this serious?
faq.a: It depends on the specific code. Some are minor and some need immediate attention.

faq.q: How much will repair cost?
faq.a: $100-$500 depending on the issue.

title: Hard Lockout - Internal Control Fault
shortDescription: Control board has detected an internal microprocessor fault.
fullDescription: Lennox E200 indicates the SureLight or Smart control board has failed an internal self-test. The unit will not respond to thermostat calls until the fault is cleared.
safetyWarning: Disconnect power at the breaker before opening control panels. High-voltage capacitors can hold a lethal charge even after power is removed.
symptoms: E200 displayed
No furnace response
Status LED off or solid

fixSteps.title: Power Cycle
fixSteps.instruction: Disconnect power at the service switch for 5 minutes, then restore.

fixSteps.title: Pro Replacement
fixSteps.instruction: Board replacement requires a Lennox dealer using model-specific parts.

whenToCallPro: Always call a Lennox dealer for board faults.

faq.q: Will my warranty cover this?
faq.a: Lennox parts warranty covers boards within the warranty period if registered.

title: Communication Fault - Indoor to Outdoor
shortDescription: Loss of communication between indoor and outdoor units.
fullDescription: On communicating systems (iComfort), E201 means the indoor furnace has lost the data link with the outdoor heat pump or AC. Operation may continue in non-communicating mode.
safetyWarning: Disconnect power at the breaker before opening control panels. High-voltage capacitors can hold a lethal charge even after power is removed.
symptoms: E201 alert
Reduced system efficiency
Stages not modulating

fixSteps.title: Inspect RSBus Terminals
fixSteps.instruction: Tighten the four communicating bus terminals on both indoor and outdoor boards.

fixSteps.title: Continuity Test
fixSteps.instruction: Verify continuity end-to-end on the comm wire run.

whenToCallPro: Persistent comm faults need a Lennox-certified technician with iComfort tools.

faq.q: Will the system still heat?
faq.a: Yes, in single-stage backup mode but without efficient staging.

title: Mismatched System Configuration
shortDescription: Indoor and outdoor units report incompatible parameters.
fullDescription: Lennox E202 occurs when the iComfort thermostat detects a system mismatch - typically after a partial equipment replacement or wiring change.
safetyWarning: Disconnect power at the breaker before opening control panels. High-voltage capacitors can hold a lethal charge even after power is removed.
symptoms: E202 displayed
Setup wizard prompts repeatedly

fixSteps.title: Run Setup Wizard
fixSteps.instruction: From the iComfort thermostat, run Setup > Equipment to re-commission the system.

fixSteps.title: Verify Dipswitches
fixSteps.instruction: Compare control board dipswitches against the installation manual for the matched coil and outdoor unit.

whenToCallPro: Capacity mismatches require professional review.

faq.q: Can I run the wizard myself?
faq.a: Yes - the iComfort wizard is designed for end users to walk through.

title: Low Pressure Switch Failed Open
shortDescription: Pressure switch did not close after inducer started.
fullDescription: E223 means the inducer is running but the low-pressure switch never closes. The unit cannot prove venting and will not attempt ignition.
safetyWarning: Involves gas combustion. If you smell gas, evacuate and call your gas utility. Only licensed technicians should service gas valves or pressure regulators.
symptoms: Inducer runs continuously
No ignition attempt

fixSteps.title: Clear Condensate Trap
fixSteps.instruction: On condensing furnaces, remove and flush the condensate trap with warm water.

fixSteps.title: Inspect Tubing
fixSteps.instruction: Check pressure tubing between switch and inducer for cracks or disconnection.

fixSteps.title: Check Vent
fixSteps.instruction: Inspect the PVC vent termination for blockage outdoors.

fixSteps.title: Test Switch
fixSteps.instruction: Use a manometer to verify negative pressure with inducer running.

whenToCallPro: If clearing the drain and vent does not resolve it, call a pro to test pressures.

faq.q: Why does the drain affect this?
faq.a: A clogged drain causes water to back up in the pressure tap, blocking the signal to the switch.

title: Low Pressure Switch Stuck Closed
shortDescription: Pressure switch closed before inducer started.
fullDescription: E224 indicates the pressure switch shows closed at the start of a heat call. The control aborts the cycle to maintain venting safety.
safetyWarning: Involves gas combustion. If you smell gas, evacuate and call your gas utility. Only licensed technicians should service gas valves or pressure regulators.
symptoms: Furnace will not start
Inducer never energizes

fixSteps.title: Replace Pressure Switch
fixSteps.instruction: Install matching OEM switch with correct trip point in inches W.C.

whenToCallPro: If new switch fails the same way, a pro should test the control board input.

faq.q: Why is this dangerous?
faq.a: A stuck-closed switch defeats the venting safety - real blockages would not be detected.

title: High Pressure Switch Failed Open
shortDescription: Two-stage furnace high-fire pressure switch did not close.
fullDescription: E227 applies to two-stage Lennox furnaces. When the unit calls for high fire, the high-pressure switch must close. If it does not, the unit drops back to low fire and posts E227.
safetyWarning: Involves gas combustion. If you smell gas, evacuate and call your gas utility. Only licensed technicians should service gas valves or pressure regulators.
symptoms: Furnace stays in low fire
Slow recovery on cold days

fixSteps.title: Inspect Vent
fixSteps.instruction: Look for ice accumulation, sagging vent runs, or screen obstructions.

fixSteps.title: Replace Switch
fixSteps.instruction: Install a new high-pressure switch matched to model.

whenToCallPro: If venting is clear and switch is good, a pro should verify inducer high-fire RPM.

faq.q: Will my furnace still heat?
faq.a: Yes, in low fire only - capacity will be roughly 70% of nameplate.

title: Flame Sensed When Not Expected
shortDescription: Flame detected with gas valve closed.
fullDescription: E240 is a serious safety fault: the flame sensor detects flame even though the control has commanded the gas valve closed. The unit locks out hard.
safetyWarning: Involves gas combustion. If you smell gas, evacuate and call your gas utility. Only licensed technicians should service gas valves or pressure regulators.
symptoms: Burner stays lit after thermostat satisfied
Possible burning smell

fixSteps.title: Shut Off Gas
fixSteps.instruction: Turn the manual gas valve to the off position immediately.

fixSteps.title: Call Technician
fixSteps.instruction: This fault requires immediate professional repair - do not operate the furnace.

whenToCallPro: Always call a pro - operating with this fault risks fire or CO buildup.

faq.q: Is this an emergency?
faq.a: Treat it as urgent - a leaking gas valve can cause overheating or unsafe combustion.

title: Rollout Switch Tripped
shortDescription: Flame rollout safety opened due to combustion problem.
fullDescription: E250 indicates the manual-reset rollout switch above the burners has tripped, sensing flame escape from the heat exchanger or burner area. The unit hard-locks out.
safetyWarning: Involves gas combustion. If you smell gas, evacuate and call your gas utility. Only licensed technicians should service gas valves or pressure regulators.

causes.cause: Blocked heat exchanger from soot or rust

symptoms: Burning smell
Visible scorching near burner box

fixSteps.title: Stop Operation
fixSteps.instruction: Do not reset the rollout switch yourself.

fixSteps.title: Pro Inspection
fixSteps.instruction: A technician must inspect the heat exchanger with a camera and combustion analyzer before resetting.

whenToCallPro: Always pro - rollout indicates a combustion issue that can produce CO.

faq.q: Is CO a concern?
faq.a: Yes - rollout often correlates with poor combustion that produces carbon monoxide.

title: Long Flame Sense Time
shortDescription: Flame sense current degraded.
fullDescription: E270 is a soft fault: the flame is being sensed but the microamp current is below the optimal threshold. The unit operates but logs the warning.
safetyWarning: Involves gas combustion. If you smell gas, evacuate and call your gas utility. Only licensed technicians should service gas valves or pressure regulators.
symptoms: E270 logged
Occasional unexpected shutdowns
Furnace runs but with periodic stalls

fixSteps.title: Polish Sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Remove sensor and polish with fine emery cloth - target a uA reading above 3.

fixSteps.title: Verify Ground
fixSteps.instruction: Inspect the ground strap from burner box to chassis.

whenToCallPro: If sensor cleaning does not raise microamps, a pro should investigate ground integrity.

faq.q: How many microamps is normal?
faq.a: Lennox typically wants 3-6 uA; below 1 uA causes lockouts.

title: Open Limit Circuit
shortDescription: Limit string open due to overheat or wiring fault.
fullDescription: E292 indicates the limit safety circuit is open. This includes the primary high-limit, auxiliary limit, and rollout switches in series.
safetyWarning: Involves gas combustion. If you smell gas, evacuate and call your gas utility. Only licensed technicians should service gas valves or pressure regulators.
symptoms: No heating
Possible past overheat event

fixSteps.title: Replace Filter, Open Vents
fixSteps.instruction: Restore airflow before further diagnosis.

fixSteps.title: Continuity Test
fixSteps.instruction: With power off, ohm out each switch in the limit string.

whenToCallPro: If airflow is good and switches read open at room temp, a pro should evaluate the heat exchanger.

faq.q: Why test all switches?
faq.a: Any single open switch in the series chain triggers E292 - you must isolate which one.

title: Integrated Control Module Internal Fault
shortDescription: The furnace control board reports an internal self-test failure.
fullDescription: This Lennox fault means the integrated furnace control's onboard self-diagnostics detected a failure — RAM/EEPROM corruption, watchdog reset, or a relay that did not transition correctly. The control halts heat operation until the fault clears or the board is replaced.
safetyWarning: Gas furnace safety: If you smell gas, leave the home immediately and call your gas company from outside. Do not operate any electrical switches. Always turn off the gas supply before attempting any repairs.

causes.cause: Voltage spike or surge damaging the control
Moisture intrusion on the control board
Failed relay or capacitor on the board
Loose ground or polarity reversed at line voltage

symptoms: Diagnostic LED steady or rapid-flashing without a normal sequence
System cycles power and resets repeatedly
Multiple unrelated faults posted at once
Furnace ignores thermostat input entirely

fixSteps.title: Hard-Reset the Furnace
fixSteps.instruction: Switch off at the disconnect for 5 minutes, then restore. A clean power-up clears most transient faults.

fixSteps.title: Verify Line Voltage and Polarity
fixSteps.instruction: Confirm 120 VAC ±10% with hot/neutral/ground correctly oriented. Reversed polarity prevents flame sensing on most boards.

fixSteps.title: Inspect Board for Damage
fixSteps.instruction: Look for swollen capacitors, scorch marks, melted relays, or corroded traces — replace the board if any are present.

fixSteps.title: Tighten All Low-Voltage Terminals
fixSteps.instruction: A loose 24 VAC connection can cause spurious resets. Snug each spade and screw terminal.

fixSteps.title: Replace the Control Board
fixSteps.instruction: Install the manufacturer-specified board, transferring DIP switch / jumper settings exactly. Confirm normal sequencing on the next call for heat.

whenToCallPro: If the fault persists after a hard reset and verification of line voltage/polarity, the board likely needs replacement by a qualified technician.

faq.q: How much does a furnace control board cost?
faq.a: Parts run $150–$500. Total installed cost is typically $400–$900.

faq.q: Will a surge protector help?
faq.a: Yes. A whole-home or HVAC-rated surge protector can prevent spike damage to the control.

faq.q: Can I swap a board myself?
faq.a: Many homeowners can, but DIP switch settings and wire routing must match exactly. Mistakes cause unsafe operation.

title: Pressure Switch Did Not Close
shortDescription: The draft pressure switch did not close within the allowed window after the inducer started.
fullDescription: This Lennox fault means the inducer motor energized but the pressure switch never sensed enough negative pressure to close its contacts. The control aborts the trial-for-ignition because operating without confirmed venting can release combustion gases into the home.
safetyWarning: Gas furnace safety: If you smell gas, leave the home immediately and call your gas company from outside. Do not operate any electrical switches. Always turn off the gas supply before attempting any repairs.

causes.cause: Blocked exhaust or intake terminal (snow, ice, debris, nest)
Plugged condensate trap on a high-efficiency model

symptoms: Inducer runs continuously without burner ignition
Furnace cycles inducer on and off chasing the switch
No heat output even though the thermostat is calling
Water dripping or pooling near a high-efficiency unit

fixSteps.title: Inspect Vent Terminations
fixSteps.instruction: Walk outside and verify the exhaust and intake pipes are clear of snow, leaves, and animal nests. Clear any obstruction with a non-metallic tool.

fixSteps.title: Check the Pressure Switch Hose
fixSteps.instruction: Remove the small rubber hose from the pressure switch, blow through it to clear water, and confirm it is firmly seated at both ends.

fixSteps.title: Service the Condensate Trap
fixSteps.instruction: On 90%+ efficiency furnaces, pour a cup of warm water through the inducer drain port to flush the trap. Reinstall and confirm free drainage.

fixSteps.title: Measure Switch Operation
fixSteps.instruction: With the inducer running, measure differential pressure at the switch port; compare to the spec on the switch (often -0.40 to -1.20 inches WC). Below spec means inducer or venting issue, not a bad switch.

fixSteps.title: Replace Inducer or Switch as Needed
fixSteps.instruction: Replace the pressure switch only if the differential pressure is correct but contacts will not close. Otherwise replace the inducer assembly with the OEM part.

whenToCallPro: If venting and condensate are clear but the switch still will not close, an inducer or board issue is likely and should be diagnosed by a licensed technician.

faq.q: Why does this happen more often in winter?
faq.a: Snow drifts and ice can block sidewall vent terminations, especially during heavy storms.

faq.q: Can I bypass the pressure switch with a jumper?
faq.a: Never. The switch is the primary safety preventing operation with blocked venting and CO buildup.

faq.q: My condensate line freezes outdoors — what now?
faq.a: Re-route the condensate to an interior drain. Frozen condensate is a common cause of repeated pressure-switch faults.

title: Ignition Failure — Hot Surface Igniter Fault
shortDescription: The hot surface igniter is not heating to the temperature needed to light the burners.
fullDescription: This Lennox furnace fault indicates the hot surface igniter (HSI) failed to reach proper glow temperature, or the control board sensed an open circuit on the igniter output. Without a glowing igniter the gas valve will not be authorized to open, so the burners never light and the cycle aborts after the trial-for-ignition period.
safetyWarning: Gas furnace safety: If you smell gas, leave the home immediately and call your gas company from outside. Do not operate any electrical switches. Always turn off the gas supply before attempting any repairs.

causes.cause: Cracked or burned-out hot surface igniter
Loose or corroded igniter wiring connection
Weak igniter — resistance drifting outside spec
Improper line voltage to the furnace

symptoms: Burners never light during a call for heat
Inducer runs but no glow visible at the igniter
Repeated retries followed by hard lockout
Cold air from registers when the blower runs

fixSteps.title: Power Cycle the Furnace
fixSteps.instruction: Switch the furnace disconnect off for 60 seconds, then back on, and watch the next ignition attempt through the inspection port.

fixSteps.title: Inspect the Igniter Visually
fixSteps.instruction: Remove the burner cover and look for a cracked, broken, or whitened igniter element. Any visible damage means replace it.

fixSteps.title: Measure Igniter Resistance
fixSteps.instruction: With power off, disconnect the igniter and measure resistance across its leads. A healthy silicon-nitride HSI typically reads 40–90 ohms; older silicon-carbide types read 50–200 ohms. Open or out-of-range = replace.

fixSteps.title: Check Igniter Connector and Harness
fixSteps.instruction: Inspect the molex/spade connector for corrosion, melted plastic, or loose pins. Reseat firmly and look for chafed wires along the routing.

fixSteps.title: Replace the Igniter
fixSteps.instruction: Install the manufacturer-specified igniter, handling only by the ceramic base — skin oils shorten igniter life. Confirm the tip aligns with the carryover slot per the service manual.

whenToCallPro: If the new igniter also fails, if line voltage is unstable, or if the control board's igniter output reads incorrect voltage during trial-for-ignition.

faq.q: How long does a furnace igniter last?
faq.a: Most hot surface igniters last 4–7 years. Frequent short-cycling and handling the element with bare fingers shorten that life significantly.

faq.q: Can I clean an igniter instead of replacing it?
faq.a: No. The ceramic element cannot be cleaned safely. If it is contaminated or cracked, replacement is the only fix.

faq.q: Why did my new igniter fail quickly?
faq.a: The most common cause is touching the element with bare fingers during installation. Skin oils create hot spots that crack the ceramic.

title: Flame Sensed Out of Sequence
shortDescription: The control board detects flame at a time when the gas valve should be closed.
fullDescription: This Lennox fault means the flame-sense rod is reporting flame current when no flame should be present — typically before the gas valve opens or after the trial-for-ignition has ended. The control treats this as a serious safety condition and locks the furnace out to prevent unburned gas accumulation.
safetyWarning: Gas furnace safety: If you smell gas, leave the home immediately and call your gas company from outside. Do not operate any electrical switches. Always turn off the gas supply before attempting any repairs.

causes.cause: Flame sensor shorted to ground or chassis
Moisture or carbon bridging on the flame-sense rod
Faulty integrated control module misreading sensor

symptoms: Furnace locks out immediately on call for heat
Burners may briefly fire then shut off with lockout
Diagnostic LED reports flame-sense fault repeatedly
No heat output despite thermostat calling

fixSteps.title: Cut Power and Inspect Burners
fixSteps.instruction: Turn off power and gas. Remove the burner cover and look for soot, water staining, or a flame sensor touching metal.

fixSteps.title: Clean the Flame-Sense Rod
fixSteps.instruction: Remove the rod and gently polish with fine emery cloth. Wipe with a clean rag — do not use sandpaper coarser than 400 grit.

fixSteps.title: Verify Sensor Mounting
fixSteps.instruction: Confirm the rod is not contacting the burner shell or any metal support. Reposition so it sits in the flame envelope without grounding.

fixSteps.title: Check for Gas Valve Leakby
fixSteps.instruction: With ignition disabled, watch the burners for any flame after the inducer purge. A momentary flame indicates a leaking gas valve, which must be replaced by a licensed pro.

fixSteps.title: Test Sensor Wiring to Board
fixSteps.instruction: Measure continuity from the sensor terminal back to the control board. Replace any harness that shows shorts to ground or open conductors.

whenToCallPro: Any time a leaking gas valve is suspected, the smell of gas is present, or the lockout returns immediately after cleaning the sensor.

faq.q: Is flame sensed when off a serious fault?
faq.a: Yes. It can mean unburned gas is entering the heat exchanger, which is a fire and CO hazard. Do not bypass the lockout.

faq.q: Can I keep using the furnace until a tech arrives?
faq.a: No. Leave the furnace off and the gas supply closed until the cause is identified.

faq.q: What is normal flame current?
faq.a: Most modern furnaces show 1.5–6 microamps of DC flame current with a clean rod and stable flame.

title: Gas Valve Circuit Fault
shortDescription: The control board cannot drive the gas valve, or its feedback is out of range.
fullDescription: On this Lennox furnace the integrated control sends 24 VAC to the main gas valve during trial-for-ignition, but the valve either does not open, draws unexpected current, or fails open-coil checks. The system locks out before any gas is released to the burners.
safetyWarning: Gas furnace safety: If you smell gas, leave the home immediately and call your gas company from outside. Do not operate any electrical switches. Always turn off the gas supply before attempting any repairs.

causes.cause: Open or shorted gas valve solenoid coil
Loose, broken, or corroded gas valve wiring

symptoms: No gas flow even with a glowing igniter
Audible relay click but no valve opening sound
Lockout posted on the first ignition attempt
Repeated retries with no flame ever established

fixSteps.title: Verify 24 VAC at Valve
fixSteps.instruction: With a multimeter on the gas valve terminals during trial-for-ignition, confirm 24 VAC ±10%. No voltage means a board or wiring issue, not a valve issue.

fixSteps.title: Inspect Valve Wiring
fixSteps.instruction: Check both leads for cracked insulation, loose spades, or green corrosion. Reseat or replace the harness as needed.

fixSteps.title: Test Valve Coil Resistance
fixSteps.instruction: With power off, measure across the coil terminals. Most 24 VAC valves read 30–80 ohms. Open or near-zero means the valve is bad.

fixSteps.title: Confirm Transformer Output
fixSteps.instruction: At the control transformer, verify 24–28 VAC under load. A weak transformer can drop voltage enough to keep the valve from pulling in.

fixSteps.title: Replace the Gas Valve
fixSteps.instruction: Replacement of the gas valve is a licensed-trade operation requiring a leak test on every joint with electronic detector and soap solution. Do not attempt without proper certification.

whenToCallPro: Replacement of any gas valve, regulator, or piping must be done by a licensed gas technician — a leak after reassembly is life-threatening.

faq.q: Can I clean a sticking gas valve?
faq.a: No. Modern valves are sealed and not field-serviceable. Replace, do not disassemble.

faq.q: How much does a furnace gas valve cost?
faq.a: Parts run $60–$220 depending on model. Professional replacement with leak test is typically $300–$700.

faq.q: Is it safe to keep using the furnace?
faq.a: If the lockout repeats, leave the system off and the gas closed. Intermittent valve faults can become hazardous quickly.

title: Open Limit Switch — Overheat Detected
shortDescription: The high-limit switch opened because supply-air temperature exceeded the safe threshold.
fullDescription: This Lennox fault posts when the high-limit switch detects supply-air temperature above the design ceiling, usually because airflow across the heat exchanger is too low. The control turns the gas off, runs the blower to purge heat, and reports the limit-trip code until temperatures normalize.
safetyWarning: Gas furnace safety: If you smell gas, leave the home immediately and call your gas company from outside. Do not operate any electrical switches. Always turn off the gas supply before attempting any repairs.

causes.cause: Severely clogged air filter restricting return airflow
Closed or blocked supply registers / collapsed flex duct
Failed or weak blower motor / capacitor

symptoms: Furnace fires briefly then shuts down
Blower runs long after the burners cut off
Hot air from supply registers followed by cold air
Burner cycle time noticeably shorter than normal

fixSteps.title: Replace the Air Filter
fixSteps.instruction: Inspect and replace the return-air filter with the correct size and MERV rating. A 1" filter clogged with dust is the single most common cause.

fixSteps.title: Open All Supply Registers
fixSteps.instruction: Walk the home and confirm every supply register is open and unblocked by furniture, rugs, or curtains. Closing too many registers raises static pressure dramatically.

fixSteps.title: Inspect the Blower Wheel
fixSteps.instruction: With power off, remove the blower assembly and check the wheel for caked dust. A coated wheel can lose 30%+ of its airflow.

fixSteps.title: Test Blower Motor and Capacitor
fixSteps.instruction: Measure capacitor microfarads and confirm they are within 6% of rated. Verify the motor reaches commanded RPM at heat speed.

fixSteps.title: Verify the Limit Switch
fixSteps.instruction: Check continuity across the limit switch at room temperature; it should be closed. If open cold, replace with the exact OEM part — limit switches are calibrated to the cabinet.

whenToCallPro: If airflow is verified normal but the limit still trips, the heat exchanger may be cracked or the gas input is overfired — both require a licensed technician.

faq.q: Can I jumper the limit switch to keep heat?
faq.a: No. Bypassing the limit can cause heat-exchanger damage and carbon-monoxide release.

faq.q: How often should I change my filter?
faq.a: Every 1–3 months for 1" pleated filters; 4–6 months for thicker media filters.

faq.q: Why does the blower keep running after lockout?
faq.a: It is intentionally purging residual heat from the heat exchanger to protect components.

title: Flame Rollout Switch Tripped
shortDescription: A flame rollout switch detected flame outside the burner enclosure and shut the furnace down.
fullDescription: This Lennox fault is one of the most serious furnace faults. A rollout switch — a one-time or manual-reset thermal device near the burner box — opened because flame escaped the heat exchanger. Causes include blocked heat exchanger, weak inducer, or cracked exchanger. Operation must not resume until the cause is identified by a technician.
safetyWarning: Gas furnace safety: If you smell gas, leave the home immediately and call your gas company from outside. Do not operate any electrical switches. Always turn off the gas supply before attempting any repairs.

causes.cause: Severely sooted or blocked heat exchanger passages
Failed or weak inducer motor (insufficient draft)

symptoms: Furnace will not restart even after power cycling
Soot or scorch marks on the burner cover
Burnt smell near the furnace
Yellow rather than blue flame at the burners

fixSteps.title: Stop Using the Furnace
fixSteps.instruction: Switch the system off at the thermostat and the disconnect. Close the gas supply at the unit shutoff. Do not attempt to reset the rollout switch.

fixSteps.title: Verify CO Detector Operation
fixSteps.instruction: Test all CO detectors on the level with the furnace. If any alarm or read above 9 ppm, ventilate the home and call for service immediately.

fixSteps.title: Document the Symptom
fixSteps.instruction: Note any soot, melted wiring, or warped sheet metal near the burners. Photos help the technician diagnose faster.

fixSteps.title: Schedule Professional Service
fixSteps.instruction: A flame rollout requires a combustion analysis, draft test, and heat-exchanger inspection — all licensed-tech work.

fixSteps.title: Do Not Bypass the Switch
fixSteps.instruction: Resetting or jumping the rollout switch without correcting the cause can lead to a fire and CO release. Wait for service.

repairTime: Professional service same-day to several days
whenToCallPro: Always. Flame rollout is never a DIY repair — there is no safe way to operate the furnace until a technician has inspected the heat exchanger and venting.

faq.q: Why is rollout so dangerous?
faq.a: Flame outside the burner box can ignite nearby materials and indicates that combustion gases — including CO — may be entering the home.

faq.q: Will the rollout switch reset itself?
faq.a: Most modern rollout switches are manual-reset only. The technician will reset after correcting the underlying issue.

faq.q: Could a dirty filter cause this?
faq.a: Indirectly. Restricted airflow over time can warp the heat exchanger, leading to cracks that allow rollout.

title: Airflow Verification Failure
shortDescription: The blower did not reach commanded RPM, indicating an airflow or motor problem.
fullDescription: On this Lennox furnace the variable-speed or ECM blower control reports that the motor failed to reach the RPM commanded by the integrated control. The system reduces firing rate or locks out to prevent heat-exchanger overheating.
safetyWarning: Gas furnace safety: If you smell gas, leave the home immediately and call your gas company from outside. Do not operate any electrical switches. Always turn off the gas supply before attempting any repairs.

causes.cause: Loose communication harness between board and motor
Incorrect blower speed configuration after install
Excessive external static pressure on duct system

symptoms: Reduced airflow at registers
Furnace cycles at lower-than-rated heat output
Blower hunts up and down in speed
Lockout posted with airflow or RPM-related code

fixSteps.title: Replace the Filter
fixSteps.instruction: Install a clean media filter rated for the airflow. Avoid restrictive 1" filters above MERV 11 unless duct sizing allows.

fixSteps.title: Measure Total External Static Pressure
fixSteps.instruction: Use a manometer at the supply and return plenum. Compare to the design value (often 0.5" WC). Higher = duct restriction problem.

fixSteps.title: Inspect Motor Communication Harness
fixSteps.instruction: Reseat the harness between the integrated control and the ECM module. Look for damaged pins or chafed insulation.

fixSteps.title: Verify Blower Configuration
fixSteps.instruction: Confirm DIP switch / dial settings for the installed tonnage and heat speed match the rating-plate guidance.

fixSteps.title: Replace the ECM Module
fixSteps.instruction: If commanded speed is correct but actual speed is far off, replace the motor module per OEM procedure. ECM motors and modules are matched pairs on many models.

whenToCallPro: If external static pressure is high, the duct system may need professional rework. ECM motor/module replacement also requires a tech.

faq.q: Why is total external static pressure important?
faq.a: It tells you whether the duct system can deliver the airflow the furnace is rated for. Too high and the blower cannot move design CFM.

faq.q: Are ECM and PSC blowers interchangeable?
faq.a: Usually not. ECM systems require a matching control output and configuration.

faq.q: Will a higher-MERV filter cause this?
faq.a: Yes if the duct system is borderline. Use thicker media filters instead of restrictive 1" panels.

title: Flame Roll-Out Switch Tripped
shortDescription: A roll-out limit detected flames escaping the burner box and tripped the manual-reset safety switch.
fullDescription: The flame roll-out switch is a manual-reset thermal safety mounted at the front of the burner assembly. When flames or hot gases escape the combustion chamber instead of being drawn into the heat exchanger, the switch trips and de-energizes the gas valve. Common causes include a blocked heat exchanger, weak draft inducer, or cracked heat exchanger.
safetyWarning: Gas furnace safety: If you smell gas, leave the home immediately and call your gas company from outside. Do not operate any electrical switches. Always turn off power and gas at the appliance shutoffs before servicing internal components.

causes.cause: Weak or failing draft inducer motor
Restricted flue or vent terminal (snow, nest, debris)

symptoms: Furnace will not light and burner area shows soot
Hot smell or scorched paint near the burner box
Manual-reset button on the burner-area switch has popped out
Repeated lockouts on cold days only

fixSteps.title: Shut Off Power and Gas
fixSteps.instruction: Turn off the furnace power switch and close the gas shutoff before opening the burner compartment.

fixSteps.title: Inspect Burner Area
fixSteps.instruction: Look for soot, scorched insulation, or melted wires around the burners — these are signs of flame roll-out.

fixSteps.title: Check Vent Terminals
fixSteps.instruction: Inspect the exhaust and intake terminals outdoors for blockage. Clear snow, nests, or debris.

fixSteps.title: Reset the Switch
fixSteps.instruction: After confirming no damage and clear vents, press the manual reset button on the roll-out switch firmly until it clicks.

fixSteps.title: Have Heat Exchanger Inspected
fixSteps.instruction: If the switch trips again, stop using the furnace and have a licensed technician perform a heat-exchanger integrity inspection.

whenToCallPro: If the switch trips a second time, the heat exchanger is suspect — call a licensed technician immediately. A cracked exchanger is a carbon-monoxide hazard.

faq.q: Can I keep running the furnace with this code?
faq.a: If the furnace still produces heat, you can run it short-term, but address the issue promptly because related safety circuits may shut it down without warning.

faq.q: Will resetting the furnace clear this?
faq.a: A power-cycle reset may clear a temporary fault, but if the underlying condition (sensor, motor, valve, vent) is still present the code will return on the next call for heat.

title: High-Limit Switch Open — Overheat Condition
shortDescription: The plenum high-limit switch opened due to excessive supply-air temperature.
fullDescription: The high-limit switch is a normally-closed thermal safety in the supply plenum. When supply-air temperature climbs above the rated limit (typically 160-200°F), the switch opens to shut off the gas valve and prevent damage to the heat exchanger. The blower continues running to dissipate heat. Repeated trips usually mean restricted airflow rather than a faulty switch.
safetyWarning: Gas furnace safety: If you smell gas, leave the home immediately and call your gas company from outside. Do not operate any electrical switches. Always turn off power and gas at the appliance shutoffs before servicing internal components.

causes.cause: Dirty or clogged air filter restricting return airflow
Closed or blocked supply registers / undersized return duct
Failed or slow blower motor (bad capacitor, bearings)
Incorrect blower speed tap for installed system

symptoms: Burners light then shut off after 1-3 minutes while blower keeps running
Supply registers feel very hot then very cool
Furnace short-cycles on heat call
Cabinet noticeably hotter than normal

fixSteps.title: Replace the Air Filter
fixSteps.instruction: Pull the filter and check for restriction. Replace any filter older than 60 days or visibly grey.

fixSteps.title: Open All Supply Registers
fixSteps.instruction: Walk the home and confirm every supply register is fully open and unobstructed by furniture or rugs.

fixSteps.title: Verify Return-Air Path
fixSteps.instruction: Check that return grilles are not blocked and that the blower-compartment door is fully sealed.

fixSteps.title: Measure Temperature Rise
fixSteps.instruction: With a thermometer, measure return and supply temperatures during a heat call. Compare against the data plate's listed rise (typically 30-60°F).

fixSteps.title: Test Blower and Capacitor
fixSteps.instruction: If temperature rise is too high, test the run capacitor and inspect the blower wheel for buildup. Replace components as needed.

whenToCallPro: If airflow is unrestricted but the limit still trips, call a technician to verify gas input pressure and check for a failing blower or undersized ductwork.

title: ECM Blower Motor Communication Fault
shortDescription: The control board has lost communication with the variable-speed ECM blower motor.
fullDescription: Modern furnaces use ECM (Electronically Commutated Motor) blowers that communicate with the control board over a low-voltage signal harness. When the board cannot read motor RPM feedback or the motor's onboard module fails to acknowledge speed commands, the system flags an ECM communication fault and falls back to either off or a fixed safety speed.
safetyWarning: Gas furnace safety: If you smell gas, leave the home immediately and call your gas company from outside. Do not operate any electrical switches. Always turn off power and gas at the appliance shutoffs before servicing internal components.

causes.cause: Loose or corroded ECM motor harness connector
Failed ECM motor control module (back of motor)
Control board ECM driver section failed
Voltage spike from recent storm or power event

symptoms: Blower will not run on heat or cool calls
Blower runs at one fixed speed regardless of mode
Audible chirping or single-rotation pulse from motor
Diagnostic code on board indicates motor / ECM fault

fixSteps.title: Cycle Power for 60 Seconds
fixSteps.instruction: Turn off the furnace breaker for one full minute to allow the ECM module to fully discharge and reinitialize.

fixSteps.title: Inspect Motor Harness
fixSteps.instruction: With power off, unplug and reseat both the 5-pin power and 16-pin control connectors at the motor. Look for burned pins or moisture.

fixSteps.title: Check Capacitor (PSC fallback models)
fixSteps.instruction: On hybrid models with a run capacitor, test it for proper microfarad rating.

fixSteps.title: Test for 120/240V at Motor
fixSteps.instruction: Confirm correct line voltage at the motor's power plug during a call for blower.

fixSteps.title: Replace Motor or Module
fixSteps.instruction: If line voltage is present and signals are correct but the motor is silent, the ECM module or motor must be replaced.

whenToCallPro: If reseating connectors does not restore communication, ECM motors must be matched to the model and replaced by a qualified technician.

title: Condensate Overflow Switch Open
shortDescription: A float or overflow switch detected high water in the condensate pan or drain trap.
fullDescription: High-efficiency (90%+) furnaces produce condensate that must drain freely. A float switch in the secondary drain pan or inline trap will open and shut down the furnace if water backs up. Common causes are a clogged condensate trap, blocked drain line, frozen drain in winter, or a failed condensate pump.
safetyWarning: Gas furnace safety: If you smell gas, leave the home immediately and call your gas company from outside. Do not operate any electrical switches. Always turn off power and gas at the appliance shutoffs before servicing internal components.

causes.cause: Clogged condensate trap with biological slime
Blocked or kinked drain hose to floor drain or pump
Failed condensate pump (motor or check valve)

symptoms: Furnace will not start; water visible in secondary pan or under unit
Gurgling sounds during inducer startup
Pressure-switch or limit faults that clear after pumping out water
Condensate pump hums but does not move water

fixSteps.title: Pump Out Standing Water
fixSteps.instruction: Use a wet/dry vac to remove water from the secondary pan and the drain trap inlet.

fixSteps.title: Clean the Condensate Trap
fixSteps.instruction: Disconnect the trap, flush with warm water and a small amount of distilled vinegar, then reinstall.

fixSteps.title: Clear Drain Line
fixSteps.instruction: Run a thin brush or shop vac through the entire drain line to the termination point.

fixSteps.title: Test Condensate Pump
fixSteps.instruction: Pour water directly into the pump reservoir; the pump should activate and discharge water within seconds.

fixSteps.title: Verify Float Switch
fixSteps.instruction: With trap clear, jumper the float switch terminals briefly to confirm operation, then restore wiring.

whenToCallPro: If the drain repeatedly clogs, a technician can re-pitch the trap, add a cleanout, or upsize the line. Frozen exterior runs may require heat tape or a redesign.

title: Line-Voltage Polarity Reversed or Open Ground
shortDescription: Control board detected reversed hot/neutral or a missing equipment ground.
fullDescription: The control board uses the chassis ground as a reference for flame-rectification sensing. If line voltage is wired with hot and neutral reversed, or if the equipment ground is open, the flame signal cannot be read reliably and the board flags a polarity / ground fault before allowing ignition.
safetyWarning: Gas furnace safety: If you smell gas, leave the home immediately and call your gas company from outside. Do not operate any electrical switches. Always turn off power and gas at the appliance shutoffs before servicing internal components.

causes.cause: Hot and neutral reversed at outlet, disconnect, or whip
Loose neutral at panel or junction box
Use of an ungrounded extension cord (temporary install)
Failed surge protector creating impedance on neutral

symptoms: Furnace will not progress past initial diagnostic
Code clears momentarily then returns when neighbor's appliance starts
Faint shock when touching cabinet (open ground)
Flame proves intermittently and drops out

fixSteps.title: Verify Power at Service Switch
fixSteps.instruction: With a multimeter on the line side of the furnace switch, confirm 120V hot-to-neutral, 120V hot-to-ground, and 0V neutral-to-ground.

fixSteps.title: Test Receptacle Polarity
fixSteps.instruction: If the furnace is cord-connected, plug a 3-light receptacle tester into the outlet to verify wiring.

fixSteps.title: Inspect Ground Wire
fixSteps.instruction: Open the furnace junction box and confirm the bare or green ground wire is firmly attached to the chassis ground screw.

fixSteps.title: Correct Wiring
fixSteps.instruction: If polarity is reversed at the outlet or disconnect, shut off the breaker and swap the hot and neutral conductors at the device.

fixSteps.title: Power Up and Retest
fixSteps.instruction: Restore power and verify the code clears and ignition completes normally.

whenToCallPro: If your service feed itself shows reversed polarity or a floating neutral, contact your utility or a licensed electrician — do not work inside the panel.

title: Communicating Bus Fault Between Thermostat and Furnace
shortDescription: The communicating thermostat cannot reliably exchange data with the furnace control.
fullDescription: Communicating systems use a 2-wire data bus (often labeled 1/2 or A/B) to exchange staging, fan, and diagnostic data between the thermostat, indoor unit, and outdoor unit. Wiring errors, polarity reversal on the data pair, or interference from a thermostat 'C-wire' adapter can break communication and force the system to a non-communicating fallback or full lockout.
safetyWarning: Gas furnace safety: If you smell gas, leave the home immediately and call your gas company from outside. Do not operate any electrical switches. Always turn off power and gas at the appliance shutoffs before servicing internal components.

causes.cause: Data wires reversed at thermostat or furnace terminal
Long wire run with too small a gauge causing voltage drop
Thermostat firmware mismatched with control board
Failed thermostat or control board communication chip
Damaged thermostat cable (staple through, rodent damage)

symptoms: Thermostat displays 'communication error', 'No comm', or blank screen
Furnace runs only on emergency / non-communicating mode
Outdoor unit will not stage up despite cold temperatures
Intermittent operation that improves after a power cycle

fixSteps.title: Power-Cycle Both Ends
fixSteps.instruction: Turn off the furnace breaker AND remove the thermostat from its base for 60 seconds, then reconnect.

fixSteps.title: Verify Wire Landings
fixSteps.instruction: Confirm the data pair lands on the matching terminals at both the thermostat and the furnace control.

fixSteps.title: Check for Damaged Cable
fixSteps.instruction: Inspect the thermostat cable along its run for staples, kinks, or chew marks. Replace any damaged section.

fixSteps.title: Update or Match Firmware
fixSteps.instruction: If the brand offers a firmware update via the thermostat menu or app, run it. Otherwise verify model compatibility.

fixSteps.title: Substitute Thermostat
fixSteps.instruction: If a known-good thermostat communicates correctly, the original thermostat is at fault.

whenToCallPro: If wiring is correct and both thermostat and board are confirmed compatible, the comm chip on the control board may be failed and require replacement.

title: Draft Inducer Locked Rotor or Out-of-Range Current
shortDescription: The control measured inducer current outside the expected range, indicating a stalled or shorted motor.
fullDescription: The control board monitors current draw on the draft inducer. When current is too low (open winding, broken connection) or too high (locked rotor, shorted winding, debris jamming the wheel), the board aborts the heat call and flags an inducer-fault code. Continuing to run a stalled motor can melt the housing or trip the breaker.
safetyWarning: Gas furnace safety: If you smell gas, leave the home immediately and call your gas company from outside. Do not operate any electrical switches. Always turn off power and gas at the appliance shutoffs before servicing internal components.

causes.cause: Inducer wheel obstructed by debris (insulation, leaves)
Loose motor wiring at control board

symptoms: Inducer hums but does not spin, or spins very slowly
Breaker trips when furnace calls for heat
Smell of hot motor windings near the inducer
Pressure switch never closes because draft is too weak

fixSteps.title: Cut Power Immediately
fixSteps.instruction: Shut off the furnace switch to prevent further damage to the stalled motor.

fixSteps.title: Check for Obstruction
fixSteps.instruction: With power off, remove the inducer cover and verify the wheel spins freely by hand.

fixSteps.title: Test the Run Capacitor
fixSteps.instruction: If the inducer uses a capacitor, measure microfarads. Replace if more than 10% out of spec.

fixSteps.title: Measure Motor Resistance
fixSteps.instruction: With leads disconnected, ohm out the motor windings; an open or near-zero reading means the motor is bad.

fixSteps.title: Replace Inducer Assembly
fixSteps.instruction: If the motor is seized or burned, replace the entire inducer assembly with the OEM part for that model.

whenToCallPro: A burned-smelling motor or repeatedly tripping breaker requires professional replacement to avoid fire risk.
